title: Iowa Department of Revenue — ARNDORFER, GRANT (O) 2026
text:
ELECTRONICALLY FILED 2026 MAR 30 9:54 AM ADMIN HEARING E-FILING SYSTEM
The appeal period has expired, pursuant to Iowa Admin. Code rule 701—7.19(8)(d) the
Administrative Law Judge’s proposed decision is final and the case is closed.
IN THE IOWA ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS DIVISION
CENTRAL PANEL BUREAU
In the matter of:
Grant Arndorfer Case No. 25IDR0001
2007 150th Street IDR Docket No. 272495
LaVerne, IA 50560,
PROPOSED DECISION
Withholding Tax.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
On October 2, 2025, a hearing in this case was held. Grant Arndorfer (“Arndorfer”) appeared; he
was represented by James Monroe. Job Mukkada and Katherine Penland (until withdrawal) appeared on
behalf of the Iowa Department of Revenue (“IDR”). Both parties presented witness testimony, and the
entire administrative file was admitted into the record, including the parties’ exhibits. At the request of the
parties, the record was held open for the parties to submit written closings, and the last reply brief was filed
on March 2, 2026. The matter is now fully submitted.
FINDINGS OF FACT
In 2020, J.A. organized and established PPG Excavating, LLC (“PPG”), for purposes of operating
a pipe laying business. Tr., at p. 35. J.A. did not possess the resources to secure financing for the company
until he convinced Arndorfer to invest in 2021 and become a minority owner in the business. Ex. S, at p.
12. The business itself appeared to have lost money until its closure in February of 2022, with it losing in
particular $38,545.03 in 2020, 151,429.26 in 2021, and $44,424,49 in 2022. Tr., at pp. 27-28. The issue in
this case whether Arndorfer is personally liable along with J.A. for the withholding tax that the business
failed to remit to IDR, and on balance, the record reveals he is primarily because, as discussed below, he
had the authority to direct payments to IDR and because he did not cause payments to IDR to be issued
despite knowing of the debt (although it should be noted he did act in subjective good faith as he thought
the issue was being handled by J.A. with a payment plan).
A.
Briefly summarizing the history of Arndorder’s involvement with PPG, Arndorfer was working as
a salesman for a company that built grain bins after having completed high school and two years of college.
Tr., at p. 108. While at this job, Arndorfer met J.A., who was also a salesman, and over time, they began
discussing J.A.’s desire to operate a pipe laying business and Arndorfer’s desire to own a business. Id., at
p. 109. Arndorfer had a $100,000.00 at the time due to working very hard since his early childhood and
being very frugal. Id. As just noted, J.A. did not have good credit or available capital to secure loans to
make the business grow, and as such, he convinced Arndorfer to invest into the business and become a
minority owner. Ex S, at p. 25 (“He had a low credit score and no real personal capital or money to put
-1 -

into this business venture, so he brought Grant in for that.”). Arndorfer was 23 at the time in 2021. Tr.,
at p. 107.
On or about April 22, 2021, PPG’s operating agreement was amended to identify both J.A. and
Arndorfer as member in PPG, with J.A. having a fifty-one percent ownership interest and Arndorfer
having a forty-nine percent interest. Ex. A, at p.1. Of note, PPC was a member-managed LLC organized
under Chapter 489 of the Iowa Code, and under the operating agreement, both members had rights of
access to all of the company’s financial records and both members had the ability to act on behalf of the
company in essentially day-to-day activities because there was no resolution limiting such, with some of
the relevant provisions from the operating agreement stating:
I. Voting Rights
Each member shall have a vote equal to the member’s percent of ownership.
. . .
III. Member Management
A. Power to Act.
The business and affairs of the Company are to be executed by its members. Every
member is an agent of the Company for the purposes of its business or affairs. The act
of member, including, but not limited to, the execution in the name of the Company and
any instrument for apparently carrying on in the ordinary course of the business or affairs
of the limited liability company shall bind the Company, unless the member so acting has,
in fact no authority to act for the Company in the particular matter, and the person with
whom the member is dealing has knowledge of the fact that the member has no such
authority.
A. Limitation on Power to Act
The following actions on behalf of the Company shall require the approval of all members. . . . No
such actions have been identified at this time.
. . . .
VI. Records
. . .
B. Location and Access
The Company’s records will be kept at the Principal Officer. Each member will have access to all
records and the Company Bookkeeper shall provide a member with copies of requested records
within five days of the request.
Ex. A, at pp. 5-8; see also Tr., at p. 98-99 (counsel for Arndorfer acknowledging there was no resolution
formally limiting member’s authority when pressed by the Tribunal on the evidence in the record).
In terms of the company’s actual operations, a shadow exists over the record because not all the
key participants either testified or had their depositions submitted and because most of the individuals that
did testify had either a motive to shade the truth or at least difficulty remembering the details of events
that occurred so long ago. Indeed, there are numerous inconsistencies between the various witnesses’
accounts, but as far as the Tribunal can discern, J.A. was dominate in the business (making essentially all
- 2 -

of the key decisions) with Arndorfer being relegated mostly to pulling together draft bids of projects and
some project management. See id., at p. 58, 111, 188-89. In fact, Arndorfer credibly testified he felt he did
not have decision-making authority in the company despite the contrary being true as a matter of law, with
him testifying:
[J.A.] made it very clear to me that his majority ownership was, you know, governing on
the decisions. Since he had that majority ownership that he had the say in everything, the
final say in everything.
Id., at pp. 119-20. It appears J.A.’s dominance was the company’s undoing, as he lacked the consistent
ability to properly bid and manage at least larger projects (with the depositions revealing he was able to do
so with at least some success on smaller matters in the past). See generally, id., at p. 113. This, along with
J.A. appropriating company resources for himself, lead to the fall of the business. At the end of the
business in February of 2022, Arndorfer and J.A. sold assets (at least some of which had financing liens)
and paid off the bank. Id., at p. 171 (“But we did end up getting that receivable late in '22, and that did
bring us whole.”). Arndorfer would then declare bankruptcy, having lost his entire investment in the
company. Id., at pp. 23, 110.
Turning in particular to the financial operations of the company, the company had L.A. and K.A.,
both relatives of J.A. at the time, keep the books and an outside CPA firm complete tax returns and provide
consultant advice. Tr., at pp. 13-14; Ex. Q, at p. 5; Ex. R, at p. 7. It also appears that the company hired a
CFO/consultant, who was its former loan officer at the bank, and the individual in short order realized
the company was not economically viable, triggering J.A. to shut the business down in February of 2022.
Tr., at p. 60. With respect to the outstanding payroll tax obligations, all agree they exist as calculated by
IDR and PPG had a failed attempt at a payment plan. Where the record is not clear is Arndorfer’s precise
knowledge of the tax obligations. According to L.A. and K.A., they thought Arndorfer would be aware
of such during his time being an owner of the business. Ex. Q, at p. 17 (““Q. Do you know if Grant ever
knew there were taxes that weren't paid? A. Oh, definitely.”), 49 (“Q. Do you recall Grant ever discussing
tax obligations to the State with you? A. I think so because those reports would have been all together.”);
Ex. R, at p. 33 (“Q Can you be any -- Do you recall anything more specific about what Grant said about
the tax debt? A. Just that he was aware of it.”). Once more the information was available on the tax return
for the company and the individual that was being brought in to be the CFO was aware of such, indicating
this information was not a secret. Appellants Exs., at p. 262; Tr., at p. 188 (“·A. Just that there were payroll
liabilities, but to the extent of how much and what and when, I'm not aware.”). When pressed on his
knowledge, Arndorfer stated he was made aware of the issue but thought it was handled with a payment
plan, testifying in particular:
Q. I can't remember if I asked you this or not, but do you ever recall [J.A.] taking $53,000
out of PPG while withholding taxes were owed?
A. I did not.
Q. You didn't authorize that?
A. Correct.
Q. When did you first become aware of withholding taxes not being paid to the State of
Iowa?
A. It would have been in the fall of 2021.
Q. September?
A. Around there, yes.
Q. And what did you do once you became aware of that?
- 3 -

A. I talked to [J.A.] and [L.A.] about it and, obviously, told them we need to address it,
and that's when they informed me that -- informed me that there was a payment plan set
up in place that the company was paying on. So at that point I was happy. I was glad they
were getting it taken care of.
Q. Did you ever have any notice or notification after that that withholding taxes weren't
being paid?
A. I did not.
Q. Did you ever receive any notices from the Iowa Department of Revenue before PPG
closed regarding ·PPG's withholding tax liability?
A. Not that I remember, no.
Q. Did you ever contact the Iowa Department of Revenue regarding withholding tax
liability of PPG?
A. No, I did not.
Q. Why not?
A. Because I didn't know the taxes were behind. To my knowledge, when the payment
plan was set up, then everything was good; everything was good to go.
Q. You thought things were taken care of at that point in time with the State; is that fair?
A. Correct.
Tr., at pp. 117-19. Of note, Arndorfer was generally not involved in payroll, but he was on the company’s
checking account and able to sign checks, which he did occasionally “whenever [J.A.] would tell [him].”
Id., at 115-16. (“Q. Did you write any payroll checks, to the best of your knowledge? A. No, I did not. Q.
Did you sign any tax returns, to the best of your knowledge? A. No, I did not”).
B.
As the business continued to decline, PPG did not remit the employment taxes as just noted,
causing IDR to send a series of Notices of Assessment to the business (not separately to Arndorfer),
assessing tax, penalty, and interest. This included a December 10, 2021, letter to the company assessing
$11,891.35 for the third quarter of 2021 ending on September 30, 2021. IDR Exs., at p. 16. This also
included a March 2, 2022 letter to the company assessing $18,334.09 for the fourth quarter of 2021 ending
on December 31, 2021. Id., at p. 12. This further included a July 15, 2022, letter to the company assessing
$6,256.10 for the first quarter of 2022 ending on March 31, 2022. Id., at p. 14. On January 24, 2023, IDR
issued a Notice of Assessment, assessing $29,737.76 against Arndorfer personally for the back withholding
taxes, and he appealed by filing a Protest claiming he “did not willfully fail to pay over withholding taxes
to the Department of Revenue.” Id., at pp. 18, 21. Of note, there does not appear to be any
communications from IDR directly to Arndorfer concerning unpaid taxes prior to PPG closing. Tr., at p.
102. (“Q: Prior to the business closing in February of 2022, are you aware of any Department
communications that were actually addressed to Mr. Arndorfer concerning delinquent taxes? A. I am not
aware.”). Also, as of February 28, 2026, the payroll taxes, penalty, and interest due September 30, 2021,
was paid off, leaving only the taxes due for the fourth quarter of 2021 and the first quarter of 2022.
Attachment AA-1.
On May 15, 2024, IDR’s appeal section denied the protest, stating in particular: “A tax is personally
liable by an owner of a business or association if the business or association failed to pay the tax on the
account.” Arndorfer Exs., at p. 28. IDR explained its position of essentially strict liability for owners of
business that fail to remit all the withholding tax on the grounds that a substantial owner must have known
or at least could have known about the financial affairs of the business and must have had the authority to
- 4 -

force the business to remit the taxes, thereby creating liability under Iowa Code section 421.26. Id. (“As a
person who invested in the business, you would become responsibility for the business and the transaction
that are associated with it. While you state that you did not make decisions for the business nor were
responsible for the day to day tasks, you had the ability to take on that responsibility and sign items within
the business.”). IDR took this position even though it has no evidence to dispute the following assertion
made by Arndorfer to it:
I was more of an investor in the business than owner. I invested $100,000 in the business
and lost it all. I was involved in the business for only about nine months. I did not make
significant business decisions. I did not pay bills or decide what bills to pay. I did not set
pay or hire new employees. [J.A.], his wife and mother-in-law handled all the financial
aspects of the business like paying bills, payroll, paying employment taxes, etc…
Exs, at p. 16; see also Tr. at, p. 84 (IDR representative stating she has no facts to dispute this statement).
The case was then transmitted to the Tribunal for hearing.
At the hearing and through closing briefs, Arndorfer argued that the assessment for the payroll
taxes for the third quarter of 2021 is effectively moot because the taxes have since been paid and because
he is not continuing any separate challenge to the initial imposition of the assessment. See Arndorfer Br.,
at p. 13 (“Based upon information and belief, PPG owes no Iowa withholding taxes for the third quarter
of 2021 due to the payments. Thus, the IDOR assessment against GA for the third quarter of 2021 should
be abated and/or invalidated.”). With respect to the first quarter of 2022, Arndorfer argues he was not a
withholding agent (a predicate to personal liability as discussed below) because he was not responsible for
the financial affairs of the company (as J.A. had the final say on all of such), J.A. routinely violated the
operating agreement and functionally froze him out of management, and he did not otherwise assume this
duty. Id., at pp. 14-16. Alternatively, he argues he had no knowledge of any unpaid payroll taxes from
this time period because the business closed as the first payments were due and he was locked out of the
company’s finances by this point. Id., at pp. 17-18. Arndorfer also argues he is not liable for the fourth
quarter payments for 2021 because he reasonably believed payments were being made on the past due
debt, which is sufficient to show no knowing violation of the law. Id., at pp. 18-19.
In response, IDR claims Arndorfer had the responsibility for tax with holdings and remittances to
IDR because: Arndorfer owned a significant share of the company; the operating agreement charged him
with operating the company as much as J.A. and authorized him to act on behalf of the company; he had
a duty to be informed about the company by virtue of the access to corporate records given to him;
Arndorfer was involved in the financial affairs of the company as evidenced by him writing checks and
L.A. and K.A.’s testimony about the information given to Arndorfer, and Arndorfer being involved in the
loans to the company. IDR Br., at p. 12-16. IDR further claims that Arndorfer knowingly failed to
complete his withholding obligations because, even by his own account he knew of the issue in September
of 2021, meaning he had a duty to investigate and remedy the tax deficiency or face personal liability. Id.,
at p. 17. IDR also notes he actually knew much more and earlier as evidenced by L.A.’s and K.A.’s
testimony, and to accept Arndorfer’s claims would produce an “absurd” result of allowing an individual to
shift the withholding duties to another, which is at odds with the governing law. Id., at p. 20.
In reply, Arndorfer focuses on the portions of the record the purportedly reveals his lack of his
actual authority and knowledge, claiming L.A. and K.A. presented untruthful testimony. Finally, it is worth
noting Arndorfer appears to have submitted proposed findings of fact in his initial brief. Submitting a
formal list of proposed findings of fact has become somewhat of an unusual procedure in recent times,
- 5 -

but to comply with the requirement that a “ruling [be issued] upon each proposed finding,” the Tribunal
will state they are rejected as either irrelevant or a misstatement of the record to the extent the proposed
finding of facts are not incorporated into the Tribunal’s findings of fact, which was arrived at by
independently viewing the entirety of the record. 701 I.A.C. § 7.18(8)(b).
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW AND ANALYSIS
A.
The basic law requiring certain individuals to withhold from wages certain payroll taxes and remit
such to the State has been established for some time and beyond meaningful contest. Indeed, by statute,
“[e]very withholding agent paying wages to an Iowa resident, or nonresident working in Iowa, shall deduct
and withhold from the wages an amount which will approximate the annual tax liability of the person on
a calendar year basis, calculated on the basis of tables to be prepared by the department and schedules or
percentage rates, based on the wages, to be prescribed by the department.” Iowa Code § 422.16(2)(a)(1).
A withholding agent is statutorily defined to include, among other things, “an officer or employee of a
corporation or association, or a member or employee of a partnership, who as such officer, employee, or
member has the responsibility to perform an act under this section and who subsequently knowingly
violates the provisions of this section.” Id. § 422.16(1). If a withholding agent fails to remit to IDR any
withheld sums required to be turned over, then the individual “shall be personally, individually, and
corporately liable to the state of Iowa.” Id. § 422.16(5). By statute, this applies specifically to “a member
or manager of a limited liability company,” and should IDR discover that a “withholding agent fails to
withhold and pay over to the department any amount required to be withheld [ ], such amount may be
assessed against such withholding agent[.]” Id. § 422.16(5), (6). A taxpayer generally bears the burden of
proof on showing any assessment is improper. See, e.g., Richards v. Iowa Dept. of Revenue, 360 N.W.2d
830, 831 (Iowa 1985)
With respect to whether a specific individual “has the responsibility” to collect and remit payroll
tax, this can be a difficult determination when there are multiple individuals involved in the ownership and
governance of a business entity. In trying to capture this difficulty, the Seventh Circuit stated when
interpreting the substantively similar federal provision:
Corporate office does not, per se, impose the duty to collect, account for and pay over the
withheld taxes. On the other hand, an officer may have such a duty even though he is not
the disbursing officer. . . . Liability attaches to those with power and responsibility within
the corporate structure for seeing that the taxes withheld from various sources are remitted
to the Government.
Monday v. United States, 421 F.2d 1210, 1214 (7th Cir. 1970). Historically, to make this determination,
IDR has relied upon the following five-factor test from federal case law:
Among the specific facts which courts have relied upon in determining whether
individuals were persons responsible for the payment of taxes withheld from the wages of
employees are:
(1) The duties of the officer as outlined by the corporate by-laws.
(2) The ability of the individual to sign checks of the corporation.
- 6 -

(3) The identity of the officers, directors and shareholders of the corporation.
(4) The identity of the individuals who hired and fired employees.
(5) The identity of the individuals who were in control of the financial affairs of the
corporation.
Braden v. United States, 318 F.Supp. 1189, 1194 (S.D. Ohio Jul. 16, 1970). The Tribunal sees no reason
to depart from this generation’s old jurisprudence, and interpreting the test, the Sixth Circuit noted:
It is well established that the test for determining the responsibility of a person . . . is
essentially a functional one, focusing upon the degree of influence and control which the
person exercised over the financial affairs of the corporation and, specifically,
disbursements of funds and the priority of payments to creditors.
. . .
Essentially, liability is predicated upon the existence of significant, as opposed to absolute,
control of the corporation's finances. . . . It is basically a factual inquiry. Generally, such a
person is one with ultimate authority over expenditure of funds since such a person can
fairly be said to be responsible for the corporation's failure to pay over its taxes, or more
explicitly, one who has authority to direct payment of creditors
Gephart v. United States, 818 F.2d 469, 473 (6th Cir. 1987).
Additional guidance on how to apply this sometimes-qualitative test can be found in IDR’s prior
decisions. In one case, IDR stated that an “individual in control of the financial affairs of a corporation
has also been characterized as any corporate officer or employee who has the power and authority to avoid
the default or to direct that withholding taxes will be paid.” In the Matter of Arthur L. Schipper, 1984 WL
138447, at *8 (citing Feist v. United States, 607 F.2d 954, 960 (Ct.Cl.1979)). Likewise, another IDR
decision stated: “So long as a person has ultimate authority over expenditures of corporate funds and
effective power to see that employment taxes withheld by employer are paid, he or she qualifies as
‘responsible person’ who may be held liable when corporate employer fails to pay over federal employment
taxes withheld from its employees.” In the Matter of: Joseph R. Higi, III, 1992 WL 471903, at *3. In
applying these factors, one decision provides some practical insight with the following analysis:
A “responsible person” is generally defined as anyone with the power and responsibility
within the corporate structure for seeing that the withheld taxes are remitted to the United
States. Monday v. United States, 421 F.2d 1210 (7th Cir.1970). As used in Sec. 6672,
“responsible person” includes every person who has significant responsibility with respect
to any one of the three functions enumerated therein. Brown v. United States, 591 F.2d
1136 (5th Cir.1979). In this case, even though plaintiff signed six checks on behalf of Land
Developers, Inc., he had no actual managerial responsibilities, functions, or authority in
Land Developers, Inc. He was not a regular signatory for checks; he did not draw or
authorize the drawing of checks; he did not sign payroll checks; and neither his signature
nor his name appears on the bank signature card for either the payroll checking account
or the general checking account for Land Developers, Inc. Moreover, there is no evidence
that plaintiff made any determination as to which creditors would be paid first. Plaintiff
Spang was clearly not a responsible person with respect to the collection, accounting for,
- 7 -

and paying over of the withholding taxes of Land Developers, Inc.
Protestor has presented substantial evidence that he had no authority to determine what
bills should be paid, or when to pay them; that he did not fill out tax forms; that he knew
nothing of what taxes had been or had not been paid; that he had no corporate
responsibility to see that withholding taxes were paid; and that he had no responsibility
for, and did nothing with respect to, the financial affairs of the corporation, except as
directed by others for the convenience of the corporation. Indeed, while Protestor held a
position on the Board of Directors and was named a vice-president, both titles, along with
a percentage interest in the corporation, were given to him in lieu of compensation; and
Protestor did not have any of his own resources invested in the company, other than labor.
In the Matter of Jerry Fangman, 1989 WL 362652, at *5–6.
With respect to the other “knowing” requirement, IDR’s prior decisions aptly summarize the test
with the following analysis:
The terminology used under the Iowa statute is “knowingly” rather than “willfully;”
however, the federal and state statutes are again, similar in their purpose, and the two terms
are fairly similar in meaning. Furthermore, the parties, in their briefs, analyze the Iowa law
concerning this issue with reference to federal cases. Thus, in determining whether or not
the Protestor “knowingly” failed to pay Iowa withholding tax, the Officer will have
reference to the federal cases defining and characterizing “willful.”
. . .
“Willfulness” has been almost universally defined as an intentional, voluntary, conscious
act or omission. In order to be willful ... it is not necessary that there be an intent to defraud
or to harm the government. One who knows that the taxes are due and the money is
available for payment but who diverts the money to creditors of the corporation has often
been viewed as having willfully disregarded the duty ... In general, willfulness can often be
shown by proving that the responsible person used money available in the corporation's
coffers for other business purposes such as payment of creditors. Feist v. United States at
p. 961.
The willfulness requirement is satisfied if the responsible person acts with a reckless
disregard of a known or obvious risk that trust funds may not be remitted to the
government ... such as by failing to investigate or to correct mismanagement after being notified that
withholding taxes have not been duly remitted. Mazo v. United States, 529 F.2d 1151, ______
(5th Cir.1977).
In the Matter of Arthur L. Schipper, 1984 WL 138447, at *9 (emphasis added). A slightly more recent case
provides additional insight and summarizes the law as follows:
“Knowingly” under the Iowa statute is similar to “willfully” under the federal law for a
withholding tax responsible party (IRC § 6672). Willfully means a voluntary, conscious
and intentional act or omission. Willful conduct also includes a reckless disregard for
obvious or known risks. Roth v. U.S., 567 F.Supp. 496, 499 (E.D.N.Y.1983); Monday v.
U.S., 421 F.2d 1210, 1215 (7th Cir.1970), cert. denied, 400 U.S. 821 (1970); Verdung v.
U.S., 84–1 USTC ¶ 9324, 83,752–53. Liability does not depend upon bad motive or a
- 8 -

specific intent to defraud the government or deprive it of revenue. Williams v. U.S., 931
F.2d 805, 810 (11th Cir.1991), modified, 939 F.2d 915 (11th Cir.1991); Roth, 567 F.Supp.
at 499; Monday, 421 F.2d at 1216.
Reasonable cause or justifiable excuses are not factors to consider in determining
willfullness. The financial condition of the business or demands of creditors are improper
and misleading factors to consider. A responsible party cannot avoid liability by evidencing
a good faith expectation that sufficient funds would be on hand on the due date for
payment to the government. The fact that a responsible party may not have paid over
withholding taxes because of creditors' demands is irrelevant to the question of willfulness.
Williams, 931 F.2d at 810–11; Verdung, 84–1 USTC at 83,752–53; Monday, 421 F.2d at
1216.
If a responsible party is aware or learns of facts which put him on notice that the corporation is delinquent
in paying withholding taxes to the government, then the responsible party has an affirmative duty to
investigate whether the taxes in fact have been paid and if they have not, to see to it that the delinquent
taxes are paid. Failure to do so constitutes willful conduct, not only with respect to taxes which have accrued
but also with respect to taxes due for subsequent periods. Verdung, 84–1 USTC at 83,753.
In the Matter of James G. Oien, 1992 WL 247032, at *8 (emphasis added). While the Tribunal may have
taken a different approach if looking at the issue without any prior guidance since knowledge is typically
viewed as a lower mens rea than willfulness, the Tribunal will follow this generations old jurisprudence unless
and until the Director of IDR decides to forge a new path (although the Tribunal will note that the analysis
from federal law as applied often looks like knowledge-level inquiry).
B.
In this case, Arndorfer has not carried his burden of proof to show the Assessment is wrong, at
least with respect to the fourth quarter of 2021 and the first quarter of 2022. As an initial matter, it appears
the third-quarter payroll taxes have been paid, which appears to moot the issue for this time period in light
of Arndorfer only challenging whether the assessment is still proper since it has been paid and not the
initial propriety of this portion of the Assessment. Arndorfer Br., at p. 14 (“Based upon information and
belief, PPG owes no Iowa withholding taxes for the third quarter of 2021 due to the payments. Thus, the
IDOR assessment against GA for the third quarter of 2021 should be abated and/or invalidated.”); see
also Attachment AA-1 (showing the tax, penalty, and interest has been paid for the period ending
September 30, 2021). As a result, the Tribunal will turn its attention to the fourth quarter of 2021 and the
first quarter of 2022.
With respect to the fourth quarter of 2021, the record established by the parties shows Arndorfer
is a withholding agent. First, at all relevant times, Arndorfer had the responsibility to perform the act of
collecting and remitting the payroll tax. This is because he was tasked with “executing” the “business and
affairs of the company” under the operating agreement, which would by law include withholding payroll
taxes, and because the operating agreement allowed him to act on behalf of the company essentially in all
of its day-to-day operations (as there was a plenary grant of authority to this effect which was not limited
by a resolution). Ex. A, at pp. 6-7. Further, he had the authorization to direct PPG to issue payments for
debts not only by the foregoing provisions in the operating agreement but also by virtue of the fact he was
already on the company’s bank account and able to write checks. There was also no legal barrier to him
hiring or firing employees, as the operating agreement would allow this generally unless a resolution passed
- 9 -

to limit his authority, which again never occurred. In fact, the factor most in dispute is the fifth factor
concerning the “identity of the individuals who were in control of the financial affairs of the corporation”
because, by all accounts, J.A. was dominate in leading the company and Arndorfer was passive if not
outright submissive to J.A. despite his legal rights to do more in the management of the company. In other
words, Arndorfer of his own volition chose to act more like a passive investor (to use the nomenclature
utilized at the hearing) and subordinate employee than an owner of the member-managed company, and
one aspect of this was him choosing to have less involvement than J.A. in the financial affairs of the
company. This decision to be passive, though, does not ultimately relieve him of being a withholding agent
because his actual authority to act on behalf of the company coupled with his responsibility to manage the
company essentially controls.
Second, the record establishes Arndorfer knowingly violated the duty to remit the payroll taxes.
According to Arndorfer, he was aware of the past-due payroll taxes at least by the Fall of 2021, specifically
around September. Arndorfer also was aware the taxes were not being full paid at the time because he
was told a “payment plan” had been instituted. While a shadow does exist on this testimony as L.A. and
K.A. indicate he was always aware of the company’s liability, it does not matter which is true because a
payment plan for back taxes does not relieve an individual of the present duty to pay all the owned taxes
in full. It is just a mechanism where IDR effectively agrees to hold off on using the various collection tools
given to it in exchange for structured sums of money that will ultimately make it whole. Because he knew
back taxes existed and because he had the right under the operating agreement to issue a check making
IDR whole at the time using the check writing authority he had, Arndorfer knowingly chose to violate the
law. In essence, and even if he did not realize it at the time, Arndorfer effectively chose which creditor
would be paid. Arndorfer’s statement he did not feel he was authorized given what J.A. had told his was
legally inaccurate and ultimately irrelevant since good faith or mistake is not a defense. In short, the record
is highly suggestive J.A. swindled Arndorfer out of his money and rights in the company, and while this is
very unfortunate, the law provides no defense for being naive or foolish in business in this context.
The same conclusion holds for the payroll taxes due in the first quarter of 2022. This is because
Arndorfer’s legal rights in the company did not change during this time and because his knowledge of the
past due taxes in 2021 put his sufficiently on notice that he had a duty to investigate and see the taxes paid
in the future, with IDR having already acknowledged from federal caselaw: “If a responsible party is aware
or learns of facts which put him on notice that the corporation is delinquent in paying withholding taxes
to the government, then the responsible party has an affirmative duty to investigate whether the taxes in
fact have been paid and if they have not, to see to it that the delinquent taxes are paid. Failure to do so
constitutes willful conduct, not only with respect to taxes which have accrued but also with respect to taxes
due for subsequent periods.” In the Matter of James G. Oien, 1992 WL 247032, at *8. If Arndorfer wants
a different outcome, he will need to explain why decades of jurisprudence should be overturned to the
Director of IDR on appeal.
In reaching this conclusion, the Tribunal rejects Arndorfer’s arguments. Arndorfer claims he did
not have the authority to issue payments to IDR, but this is factually untrue given the authority given to
him in the operating agreement. Even if he faced some resistance in fact by J.A. and others, Arndorfer
had the legal right to force the action. This is true even after the company started its winding up process
in February of 2022. Again, J.A. never actually called a company meeting and issued a resolution with his
majority share to limit Arndorfer’s legal authority under the operating agreement. Arndorfer also claims
that his duties in the company did not include managing the financial affairs of its, as he exercised no
independent judgment whether it be what checks to issue or even what a final bid would be to a potential
client. However, the operating agreement made no such distinction, and given his legal rights act on behalf
- 10 -

of the company, his knowledge of tax debt by September of 2021 means he had a choice to either see the
debt paid (and confirm such) or face personal liability. As just stated, there were only two members of
PPG, and he had a significant share with significant authority that was never cut down be resolution. J.A.’s
threats to do so never materialized. As such, and frankly while it is appears Arndorfer’s naivety and/or
strong desire to be a business owner blinded him to appreciate the significance of the state of PPG and
what was occurring, there is nothing the Tribunal can do but AFFIRM the portions of the Assessment
Arndorfer is still challenging. The law as applied is designed to avoid the result Arndorfer want.
ORDER
IDR’s action is AFFIRMED. Interest continues to accrue at the statutory rate, and IDR shall
take all necessary action to implement this decision.
IT IS SO ORDERED.
